You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.
(One of the texts is a real LinkedIn post by a person, written on its own topic; judge tells, not topic.)

=== TEXT A ===
Too much #Lean can undermine your product efforts.
 
Stop applying it without reflection.
 
Lean puts much emphasis on reducing waste and costs. If product managers focus on it too much, things go terribly wrong.
 
Let's look at two areas of waste in lean manufacturing:
 
1. Unused talent ("underutilization of people")
 
Knowledge work is different from work on the production line. 100% utilization is never a good solution. The inevitable multitasking and constant context switching can drastically lower people's productivity.
 
We don't get paid for being fully utilized (feature factory). We get paid for delivering valuable outcomes. To do that, we need time to pause and think.
 
You should be "utilized" at about 50 to 60 percent to provide maximum value for your organization. More than that is a waste of talent.
 
2. Extra-processing
 
Lean defines extra-processing as quality higher than required by the customer. It makes sense for screws or chairs. The product fulfills its function, which may be the only thing customers expect.
 
In #productmanagement, we need a different approach. Think about iPhone. Do people buy it only to make calls or take photos? Emotional and social outcomes can be more important than the core functionalities of the product.
 
Customers don't just want their needs to be met. They want to be delighted.
 
-
 
Don't get me wrong. Lean and #Agile can coexist. But it's important to remember that Lean comes from manufacturing. We should use it carefully.
 
#Scrum doesn't implement Lean in its entirety. In my opinion, you shouldn't either.
 
What are your thoughts? Let me know in the comments.

=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Six months ago, we shipped a feature I was certain would change how our customers worked.

It was a customizable dashboard. Users could drag widgets around, pick their own metrics, save multiple layouts. We'd heard "I wish I could see X next to Y" in enough support tickets that it felt like an obvious win. Three engineers, two months, a design sprint, a launch email with a little animated GIF.

Adoption after 90 days: 2.1%.

Not "2.1% used it daily." 2.1% opened it once.

I spent a week feeling defensive about it. Then I actually went and talked to the people who'd asked for it. Here's what I learned.

**People weren't asking for customization. They were asking for a specific answer.**

When someone said "I wish I could see X next to Y," they didn't want a drag-and-drop canvas. They wanted X next to Y. Every single one of them wanted the *same* X and the *same* Y. We heard a request for flexibility and built infrastructure for infinite flexibility, when a single hardcoded view would have solved 80% of the problem in three days.

**Requests describe symptoms, not solutions.**

We took the literal words in the tickets and shipped them back. We never asked the one question that mattered: "What are you trying to decide when you look at this?" If we had, we'd have discovered they were all trying to figure out whether to escalate an account before a renewal call. That's not a dashboard problem. That's an alert.

**"Configurable" often means "we didn't want to make the call."**

I've come to see customization features as a yellow flag in my own thinking. Sometimes they're the right answer. But often they're a way of handing the hard product decision to the user, dressed up as empowerment. Our customers didn't want to design their own tool. They wanted us to have already figured it out.

**Low adoption isn't a marketing problem.**

Our first instinct was to promote it harder. In-app tooltip, another email, a webinar. That would have been spending more to defend a decision instead of learning from it. If something genuinely solves a pain point, people find it. Adoption campaigns are for things people don't know they need, not for things they don't need.

What we did next: we killed the customizable dashboard. Replaced it with one fixed view showing the two metrics everyone actually wanted, plus a notification when an account crossed a risk threshold. Took a week and a half.

Usage of that view is now higher than any other page in the product.

I don't regret shipping the thing nobody used. It's the most expensive product lesson I've had, and I'd rather have paid for it once than keep making the same mistake in smaller ways forever.

The lesson, if I had to compress it: when a customer tells you what to build, thank them, then ask what they're trying to do. Build that instead.

Curious whether others have a "feature nobody used" story. What did yours teach you?
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Rhetorical question followed by answer ('Think about iPhone. Do people buy it only to make calls...? Emotional and social outcomes...')
tells_B: Heavy reliance on negative parallelism ('People weren't asking for X. They were asking for Y', 'They didn't want a drag-and-drop canvas. They wanted X next to Y', 'That's not a dashboard problem. That's an alert', 'not for things they don't need')
Signposting ('Here's what I learned.', 'What we did next:', 'The lesson, if I had to compress it:')
Bold-label paragraph openers formatted as standalone punchy maxims for every section
Triad structure ('In-app tooltip, another email, a webinar')

Neat, uplifting resolution where every point lands perfectly and failure leads to instant, massive success ('Usage of that view is now higher than any other page')
